title: Transitions
lede: Transition words tell the reader how one idea connects to the next.

sections.md:
## Transitions by job
| Job | Words |
|---|---|
| Add | also, in addition, moreover, furthermore |
| Contrast | however, but, on the other hand, yet |
| Cause and effect | because, so, therefore, as a result, consequently |
| Example | for example, for instance, such as |
| Sequence | first, next, then, finally |
| Conclude | in short, overall, in the end |

## Use the right one
A transition is a promise. "However" promises a contrast; "therefore" promises a conclusion. Using the wrong one confuses readers even when every sentence is fine.

sections.label: Punctuation with however and therefore
sections.md: These aren't joining words like "but." Use a period or semicolon before them: "Rates rose; **however**, volume held steady."

sections.title: Fix the connection
sections.problem: "Fuel went up 20%. We raised our rates."
steps: The second sentence is a result of the first.
sections.answer: "Fuel went up 20%. **As a result**, we raised our rates."

practice.q: "Many costs are fixed. ___, insurance and truck payments don't change with miles."
practice.why: It gives examples of fixed costs.
